commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: Feature lanes — isolated worktree + port + hostname, one command each
commits.body:
One machine is the source of truth and is reached over SSH from several
computers, so a preview lane cannot belong to a shell session and cannot be
identified by "the one on 3051". A lane's name derives all of it:

  packed-pie -> ~/Projects/cycleforge-lanes/packed-pie   (detached at main)
             -> :3071                                    (allocated once)
             -> https://packed-pie.michaelgarisek.com
             -> cycleforge-lane@packed-pie{,-tunnel}.service
             -> ~/.config/cycleforge/lanes/packed-pie.env

`~/.config/cycleforge/lanes/` IS the registry — systemd reads those files
natively as EnvironmentFile, so there is no second copy to drift. Two templated
units serve every lane forever; `pnpm lane doctor` reinstalls them from
`ops/systemd/`.

Deliberate choices:

- **systemd --user, not tmux.** Survives the SSH disconnect, returns after a
  reboot (lingering is already on), and `pnpm lanes` reads identically from
  every machine. Crash-loop backstop matches cycleforge-dev.service.
- **A locally-managed tunnel per lane.** `usav-dev` is REMOTELY managed — its
  ingress lives in the Cloudflare dashboard and wins over any local file — so a
  lane gets its own named tunnel and its own config. The explicit `--config` in
  the unit is load-bearing: without it cloudflared reads usav-dev's.
- **No branches.** Lane worktrees are detached at main; `lane land` is
  `merge --ff-only` + push, guarded on: lane committed, lane ahead of main,
  verify green IN THE LANE, and the MAIN checkout clean (other sessions edit
  that tree).
- **Nothing here touches :3050 or cloudflared.service.** `lane up`/`down` act
  only on `cycleforge-lane*@<name>`.

Known gap, documented rather than hidden: `cloudflared` can create a DNS route
but not delete one, so `lane rm` tears down the tunnel and worktree and then
tells you to remove the CNAME by hand.

Also lands PLAN-filter-well-sot.md — the one-feed/two-faces filter contract,
its port waves, and the nine steps to verify Wave 0.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: Add a design-system MCP server for CycleForge
commits.body:
Three tools over stdio, auto-discovered via .mcp.json: ds_contract (what
already exists for this job), ds_tokens (what values are allowed), ds_critique
(why is this component bad).

## The contract is derived, not written

Garisek's server reads a hand-curated pin map with useWhen/doNot per entry. This
repo has no such file and its primitives carry no docblocks to derive those
sentences from — Button.tsx opens straight into imports. Writing 56 doNot rules
from outside would be inventing law and serving it with authority, which is the
one failure a design-system oracle must not commit.

So ds_contract reports what the repo can prove: all 56 primitives, where they
live, their real variant options read from source, and the interaction states
they declare. Curated prose layers on from src/design-system/pinned.json when it
exists — optional, absent today, grown one justified entry at a time. The
response states explicitly that an absent useWhen means nobody has written the
law yet, NOT that anything is permitted.

## Two primitive homes are reported, not resolved

src/design-system/primitives (40) and src/components/ui (16) both hold
primitives — there are two Buttons with different variant surfaces. That is a
real open question in this repo; the server labels both so an agent sees the
choice rather than picking whichever it grepped first.

## No ds_adjudicate

Garisek's shares a rule module with a PreToolUse hook, so its verdict is the one
that blocks a write. Nothing equivalent exists here, and a tool answering
"allowed" while nothing enforces anything manufactures confidence. ESLint is the
gate; the header says where an adjudicator would plug in.

## The extractor was wrong twice before it was right

Both are now pinned as exact counts in the smoke test:

- It anchored on `_VARIANTS`, which also matches Button.tsx's own IMPORT line,
  sending the brace-matcher into the import braces — the flagship primitive
  reported zero variants while a sibling file declared nine.
- It understood only the cva `variants: { axis: { opt } }` shape and missed flat
  maps (`BUTTON_VARIANTS = { primary: '…' }`) entirely. Now a key is an axis
  only when its value opens a block; if none do, the map is one axis.

Ground truth checked by hand: 9 flat variants on the design-system Button,
6 variants x 4 sizes on the ui button. Smoke test is 11 assertions over real
stdio, including a refused path traversal and fork detection staying off inside
the primitive homes.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: perf(tooling): make the request-shape audit repeatable
commits.body:
The receiving/unbox network audit landed as a one-off. This turns the method
into something any route can be put through.

`npm run perf:requests -- --route=/x` signs in via the pinless flow, drives
Playwright against a production build, and reports the four axes the audit was
organised around: depth (serially dependent round trips), width (peak
concurrency), redundancy (identical URL, or one endpoint under several param
shapes), and poll-vs-push (what a window-focus regain re-fetches). It writes a
JSON baseline per route so a before/after is a file diff rather than a
recollection.

Three things the tool had to learn the hard way, all encoded:

- It refuses to run against a dev server. Dev does not report a slower shape,
  it reports a DIFFERENT one — StrictMode double-invokes effects, so every raw
  fetch-in-useEffect appears twice and the redundancy column is fiction. The
  two detection signals were verified positive on :3050 and negative on the
  live production build, because a false positive would refuse a real run.
- The depth column is labelled DEPTH? and pairs each request with only its
  closest candidate parent. The first version reported one photo request
  chained to three unrelated parents: from outside the app, co-timing is
  indistinguishable from causation.
- Totals are noisy (43 vs 51 requests across back-to-back runs of one build);
  the duplicate and count-probe columns were identical every time. The skill
  says to quote those as findings and treat the headline as order-of-magnitude.

The skill also carries the suspects already ruled out on this codebase (Ably
connection count, catalog hook dedup, the retired serial-hydration N+1) so they
are not re-derived, the RSC-seed gate that /triage failed, and the two misses
from the original audit: that a caller which exists is not a caller that fired,
and that reporting a failed gate is completing the item.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: perf(ci): two-tier performance gate, and fix the measurement it depends on
commits.body:
Target is Lighthouse >=90 in every category on every route. Only Performance is
short: A11y 93-95, BP 96, SEO 91, CLS ~0 and TBT 22-158ms already clear it.
Performance sits at 67-78 and the entire gap is LCP (5.9-12.3s) on the five
data-heavy workbenches that render a shell, hydrate, then fetch their first
collection. Bundle weight was already cut 61-68% and is not the constraint.

Fix the instrument first — two bugs were distorting every number:

1. lhOptions set `formFactor: 'desktop'` but never set `throttling`. Lighthouse
   derives only screenEmulation from form factor; throttling defaults to
   mobileSlow4G regardless. So /unbox, /test and /kiosk* were measured at a
   desktop viewport over a phone's cellular link with 4x CPU slowdown — a device
   that does not exist. Throttling now follows the form factor.
2. The other five desk workbenches were never pinned at all. This is a warehouse
   management system: sheet/grid workbenches run on LAN workstations, /m/* is the
   handheld tree, /kiosk* is a mounted tablet. All 22 routes now declare the
   hardware they ship on (15 desktop, 7 mobile, 0 unpinned). /signin stays mobile
   as the public worst-case canary.

Scores only compare within one profile, so the baseline records formFactor and
--check now fails loudly on a profile mismatch instead of silently passing floors
measured under different conditions. lighthouse-baseline.json is marked stale for
exactly that reason — it must be re-seeded. A route with no baseline entry now
fails too; an unpinned surface is a coverage hole, not a pass.

CI (.github/workflows/performance.yml), two tiers by cost:
- bundle-budget — every PR + push. One build, then Next's own First Load JS table
  ratcheted against bundle-budget.json. Deterministic, no browser.
- lighthouse — nightly + workflow_dispatch. Build, server, minted session,
  median-of-3 over Tier 1. 30-60 min, so it stays off the commit path.

Budgets parse the printed build table rather than .next/app-build-manifest.json,
which Turbopack does not emit. Ceilings only move DOWN. Both jobs skip with a
warning when PERF_DATABASE_URL is absent, so an unconfigured repo does not carry
a permanently red check.

Also: lighthouse-audit.mjs exports ROUTES, but called main() unconditionally, so
importing the manifest launched Chrome and audited all 22 routes. Guarded.

Note: `npm run verify` is red in the working tree from another session's
in-flight search-recents work (one TS2307 on a file it added then deleted).
Nothing here touches TypeScript under src/.

commits.subject: feat(loader): eight pastels, chosen by what reads on white
commits.body:
The field's colour used to be `--ds-color-accent-bg` — the per-STAFF
accent — so the whole loader was one operator's colour and every dot in
it was the same hue. It is now eight base families, and the palette can
no longer collapse back to one: `has enough hues` pins the floor.

Adds green and yellow, but NOT at `-300` like the other six. Composited
over white at IDLE_ALPHA they land at 220 and 226 against a 183–213 band
— lighter than every existing family, so at `-300` they wash out on the
plane while their neighbours read fine. They rest at `-400` instead.

The invariant is therefore the LUMINANCE BAND, never a fixed step
number, and `palette-reads-on-white` asserts it: adding a ninth family
means picking the step that lands in the band, not copying `-300` and
hoping. `luminanceOnWhite` is exported so the test measures the same
function the field does.

The pre-hydration CSS lattice now samples ACROSS the palette instead of
taking the first four, so it previews the real spread and the handoff to
the canvas is not a visible widening of the range.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: feat(loader): the loading field is pastel on a white plane
commits.body:
The plane is now a fixed `bg-white` in every theme rather than
`bg-surface-canvas` — operator ruling. This is the one place the field
steps outside the theme layer, which is also why its palette moved from
the semantic tokens to `baseColors`: pastels tuned for white would be
wrong over a dark plane, so the plane is pinned instead of the palette
chasing it. On a dark theme this reads as a bright white card while a
surface loads.

Dots wear one of six `-300` pastels and deepen to their own `-500` under
the sweep or the pointer. Deepening stays inside the family on purpose —
blending across families sends a green dot through grey on its way to
blue, and a field full of that reads as dirty rather than as pastel.

Hue comes from a spatial xor-hash, not `(a·col + b·row) % n`. Every
linear form lays the palette out as a lattice, and since the sweep front
runs along `x + y` the regular ones are exactly the wrong shape: colour
by that sum and every instant of the wave is one solid hue.

IDLE_ALPHA 0.6 → 0.8. A `-300` pastel at 0.6 over white lands near
rgb(190, 220, 254), and once antialiasing has thinned a sub-pixel circle
the eye reads that as grey — a pastel field whose pastels do not register
is just a grey field. Raise opacity before radius; the dots stay fine.

Drops the runtime token reader and the `data-theme` MutationObserver:
with a static base palette there is nothing left to re-read.

commits.subject: feat(scan): global scan dock — a scan input that survives navigation
commits.body:
Infrastructure for moving the station scan bar into GlobalHeader. Renders
nothing until a surface publishes a policy, so mounting it is inert and surfaces
migrate one at a time.

The defect is a REMOUNT, not a layout. Every station bar lives inside its
surface's sidebar panel, and those panels are swapped by component identity:
TechSidebarPanel renders TestingSidebarPanel OR ShippingSidebarPanel depending on
the mode, so React unmounts one and mounts the other. The input goes with it —
value, focus, and the DOM node. On the QC → Ready to Pack jump this router
performs, the operator's cursor lands nowhere.

GlobalHeader is mounted once by ResponsiveLayout, which lives in the ROOT
layout, and the App Router never remounts that across a client navigation. An
input mounted there survives every jump.

It is a FOURTH header zone, deliberately not panelContent. That middle slot is
republished by each page through useHeader() — it is the one part of the header
that does churn per route, so putting the bar there hands back the remount the
dock exists to escape.

The dock owns the input; the surface publishes policy (placeholder, onSubmit,
staff theme, and its mode rail as a node so migration is lossless — folding
every station's modes into one dock-owned union would be the twin this design
avoids). On a policy change it clears the VALUE and keeps the FOCUS: focus
continuity is the point, while carrying a half-typed serial from Quality Control
to Ready to Pack would hand the next bench a string its resolver never saw
scanned.

This deletes plan phase P2 in full — ?scanArm= and armPendingTarget() existed
only to re-focus a bar that had remounted.

NOT YET MIGRATED. Tech is the intended golden, but it is a visible change to a
live bench and wants eyes on the screen rather than a green typecheck. Migration
recipe: plan section 7.

commits.subject: feat(scan): seed the whole command vocabulary per org, and fix the seeder
commits.body:
Makes all 27 codes visible, relabellable and printable in Admin > Reason Codes
(flow_context = 'station_command'). Behaviour stays code-owned: a row here arms
nothing.

The real bug was in the per-org seeder, not the missing rows. seedOrgCatalog —
the path that runs on org creation and signup — iterated STATION_COMMAND_CODES
alone. Correct when those two session codes WERE the whole vocabulary, and
silently wrong the moment a second registry existed: every code added to the nav
or action registry would have been invisible for every new org, forever, with
nothing able to notice, because the seeder was not wrong about anything it knew
about. It now derives from listSeedableCommandCodes(), a union of all three
registries, so new orgs are correct by construction. A migration backfills the
past; the derived seeder is what keeps the future right.

2026-08-20d backfills the 25 new codes for every existing org with ON CONFLICT
DO NOTHING, so a row a tenant may have relabelled is never stomped.

2026-08-20e exists because verifying 20d showed its own header was wrong. It
predicted the two 2026-08-04 session rows would keep sort_order 10/20 and simply
"sort above" the new codes — accepted. They did not sort above, they TIED:
CMD-BATCH-SORT and CMD-GO-ARRIVAL both at 10, ordered arbitrarily by the
planner. An admin list whose order changes between reads is worse than one with
an odd but stable order. The correction updates only rows still holding their
exact original seeded value, so a tenant who deliberately reordered is untouched
— the same reasoning that made 20d use DO NOTHING, applied precisely rather than
bluntly.

Applied and verified against the live DB: 27 codes across all 8 orgs, zero
sort_order ties.

Guard: command-seed-coverage.test.ts asserts the seedable list equals the
registered set, that sort orders are unique and ascending, and that every
registered code appears in SOME station_command seed migration. That last is a
union across migrations rather than one named file — an applied migration is
immutable (the ledger is keyed on sha256), so code #28 gets a new migration and
failing this test is the prompt to write it.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: feat(scan): custom codes are aliases, and only aliases
commits.body:
A tenant can name its own scan string — CMD-GO-BENCH-3 → CMD-GO-QC — and that
is the whole of what a custom code may do. An alias resolves to its TARGET, and
everything downstream (permission gate, destination, verdict) is decided by the
target, so an alias can rename a jump and can never widen one. The registries
stay code and PR-reviewed, because a scan that moves an operator or writes a
verdict must not be creatable from an admin form.

The namespace rule is a safety control. `code` must match
^CMD-[A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9-]*$, enforced by a DB CHECK and by validateAlias — the same
function the form uses, so it cannot accept what the route will refuse. The
classifier claims CMD- wholesale so a command is never read as a serial, and an
alias outside it breaks that in BOTH directions: BENCH-3 would classify as a
serial fragment and be looked up against tech_serial_numbers, and a real serial
shaped like the alias would silently trigger a station jump. Shadowing a
built-in is refused separately — it would make the built-in unreachable by its
own printed sticker, and every book already bound in the building would be wrong.

Two resolutions, one authoritative. The client hydrates once per session and
resolves synchronously, because a bench scan that waits on the network is a scan
the operator out-runs. The server re-reads from the DB on every write: a `code`
arriving at /api/stations/handoff is a wire value, and trusting the client's
resolution would let a caller name any command it liked by claiming an alias for
it. The client's copy is a latency optimisation; the server's is the gate.

A table, not a reason_codes column. Commands are already seeded into
reason_codes for Admin visibility and print, but an alias carries a target and
no other row in that table would ever use one — alias_target there would be a
discriminator-shaped column with no discriminator, NULL on every other
vocabulary. The vocabulary stays in reason_codes; the mapping lives here.

DELETE is a soft retire. A printed sticker outlives its row, and an operator
scanning a retired one deserves "this code was retired" rather than the generic
unknown-command nack — the row is what lets us say that.

Migration 2026-08-20c is tenant-from-birth (org-led unique index,
enforce_tenant_isolation, FORCE RLS) and ships with its Drizzle model in the
same change, per expand-first.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: feat(scan): the command book — a printable catalog you scan off the page
commits.body:
/settings/commands renders every CMD-* string grouped by what a scan DOES: Go
(safe anywhere), Do (writes — scan the unit first), Mode (arms this bench). That
grouping is the only distinction that changes how an operator may use the page.

Row anatomy is the printed label's, turned sideways and enlarged: text on the
left, matrix on the right — the same slot order as LabelFaceModel and the unbox
carton face, so anyone who can read a carton label can read a book row. Print
book emits the whole thing in one job with break-inside-avoid, because half a
matrix is unscannable and half an instruction is worse. Each row keeps a 2x1"
sticker button through the existing printStationCommandLabel.

Symbology is datamatrix, not QR. Every carton, unit, bin and repair label in
this app already carries DataMatrix and the floor's guns are configured for it;
a second symbology for one document is a scanner-configuration problem disguised
as a design choice. Matrices are 128px — a book is read at arm's length off a
flat page, not pressed against a carton like a 2x1" sticker.

The book cannot drift from the parser. It is assembled from the three
registries, and command-book.test.ts asserts the printed set EQUALS the
registered set and that every printed code actually parses. A laminated page
that teaches a code the app refuses is worse than no page.

Composed, not forked: the 2x1" face (printStationCommandLabel) prints one
sticker per job on thermal stock. A book is a different artifact — many codes,
one paper job, read at distance — so it reuses the same registry and the same

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: feat(scan): pass-and-move — the one place a scan may change status
commits.body:
Scan a unit, then scan CMD-PASS-GO-READY: the verdict is recorded and the
operator lands on Ready to Pack. Three verdict-only codes (CMD-PASS / CMD-FAIL /
CMD-TEST-AGAIN) and three compounds.

The write composes recordTestVerdict, NOT transition(). The plan said
transition() and that was wrong: recordTestVerdict is the QC verdict SoT and
also owns the tech_serial_numbers row, the testing_results feed, the parent line
rollup and the workflow tap. Calling transition() raw would move the unit's
status while none of that happened — worse than not shipping the sticker.
POST /api/stations/handoff is therefore a sibling of
POST /api/serial-units/[id]/test, not a replacement: that route takes an id from
the URL and a verdict from the body (a pointer gesture), this one takes a
scanned KEY and a sticker CODE (a scanner gesture) and answers with where to go
next. Both delegate to the same helper, so a verdict by sticker and one by
button are the same event — distinguished only by method:'scan' in the audit row,
which is the only place that can say which gesture an operator performed.

A navigation sticker never writes. That split is the safety model, not tidiness:
a status change on a scan whose face says only "go" is a change nobody named,
and the operator sees a page turn with no way to know a unit moved lifecycle
underneath it. The compound spells out both halves, so the sticker's face is the
disclosure.

CMD-FAIL lands ON_HOLD, not IN_REPAIR as the plan's table claimed.
VERDICT_TO_STATUS maps TESTING_FAILED → ON_HOLD, and hold is where a failed unit
waits for someone to choose repair or scrap. CMD-FAIL-GO-REPAIR moves the
OPERATOR to Repair to make that call; inventing a second status path so the code
matched a sentence would have forked the verdict SoT to save a doc edit.
CMD-SCRAP / CMD-HOLD are not verdicts at all and are deferred rather than
smuggled through the verdict endpoint.

The subject — the unit a verb sticker acts on — is a one-slot module store with
a 2 minute TTL. A subject with no expiry is a loaded gun on a shared bench: scan
a unit, walk away, and someone else's verdict sticker lands on it. It is cleared
on consume so a double trigger-pull cannot re-apply a verdict, with
clientEventId threading to inventory_events.client_event_id as the second line.
Only a SERIAL becomes a subject: a tracking number or carton handle names work,
not a unit, and a verdict landing on one would have to guess which unit inside
it was meant.

Navigation happens only on a 2xx. A failed write that still moved the operator
would leave the bench believing work landed that did not; a 409 from the
transition guard nacks in place.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: feat(scan): universal scan router — CMD-* jump stickers at every scan bar
commits.body:
Turns the station scan bar from a per-surface receiving control into the one
system-wide scan waist: a printed `CMD-GO-*` sticker moves the operator between
surfaces, from any bench, without touching a mouse.

Nineteen codes, keyed to SIDEBAR_PAGE_NAV page + child ids rather than literal
URLs — that registry already owns every route, its ?view=/?mode= delta and its
permission gate, so a sticker inherits all three instead of forking a fourth
copy of the vocabulary. Destination URLs are built by applyChildTarget, so param
isolation is inherited: CMD-GO-READY clears a stale ?view=testing but keeps a
?staff= filter the operator set by hand.

The permission is DERIVED (child.requires ?? page.requires), never declared on
the command. A hand-copied gate is a second answer to a question the nav graph
already answers, and the copy goes stale silently — the page's gate changes, the
sticker keeps the old one, and a jump is refused for an operator who should have
it or allowed for one who should not. A refused jump nacks at the bar and stays
put rather than stranding the operator on /not-authorized.

Fixes a live defect while it is here. detectStationScanType hardcoded
['YES','USED','NEW','PARTS','TEST'] and never consulted parseStationCommand, so
CMD-BATCH-SORT — already shipped and in use on Arrival — fell through the whole
cascade to classifyInput and came back SERIAL. At the tech bench that was a
candidate to be persisted into tech_serial_numbers as a unit identity. The CMD-
namespace is now claimed wholesale and read FIRST: an unregistered CMD-* answers
COMMAND and gets nacked rather than guessed at. The namespace check stays narrow
(`CMD-` with a real hyphen, plus squashed `CMDGO…`) so a manufacturer serial
beginning CMD is not swallowed — trading a missed sticker for a swallowed serial
is not a fix.

Claimed at two waists. StationScanBar's submit is the one every station bar
shares, and it is the only place a scanned CMD-* can be caught when focus is in
the field (the wedge listener stands down over editable targets) — catching it
once there is what makes all ~20 hosts inherit the vocabulary. The global wedge
listener covers a scan landing on a row or chrome, placed AHEAD of the page
claimers because Unbox History buckets anything it cannot decode as search text
and would have typed a jump sticker into a filter box.

Codes are [A-Z0-9-] only and resolve from their squashed form, so they survive
an HID wedge running the wrong keyboard country — the same failure that produced
the FLATTENED_MOBILE_LINK_RE recovery arm in barcode-routing.

commits.subject: fix(motion): the overlay hard-cut flag commits in an effect, not during render
commits.body:
`/unbox` logged a React hydration mismatch on every cold load. Four station
overlays each derived "is the overlay already open?" by assigning a ref on the
line after reading it:

    const hardCut = showOverlay && wasOpenRef.current;
    wasOpenRef.current = showOverlay;          // <- during render

That makes the render answer depend on how many times React ran the body.
The dev double-invoke re-runs it with the ref already advanced, so pass 1
answers false and pass 2 answers true. `/unbox` server-renders its overlay
open on cold land, so the split landed as a real mismatch — server
`z-index: 100`, hydrating client `zIndex: 101`, "won't be patched up" — and
the same one flag also flipped `mode` (wait -> sync) and `initial`.

One hook now answers it for all four (Unbox, Triage, Packer, Tech) and commits
the previous-open flag in an EFFECT. The mount render — the only one hydration
compares — answers false, which is what the server emitted and what
`AnimatePresence initial={false}` already renders un-animated. Every render
while the overlay stays open still answers true, so the zero-flash carton→carton
cover-replace is unchanged; React flushes passive effects before beginning the
next render pass, so a swap cannot observe a stale flag.

Pinned by a mounted test (jsdom + createRoot), including a StrictMode pass:
restoring the old shape fails that case and only that case. Verified in the
browser against the QA org — the console error is gone and the pane still
carries z-index 101 while open.

commits.subject: feat(receiving): one pending-work card for follow-up owed after the scan
commits.body:
Rung 0 (the nas_archived_* stamp) and rung 1 (the amber ticket chip) landed
in 846d7e77b. This is the registry they were always heading for.

WHY A CARD AT ALL. A photo taken on a ticketed carton, or an exception raised
at the door, is follow-up the operator owes. The surfaces that carry those
facts — the ticket chip, a Displays leaf — unmount the moment the next box is
scanned, which is exactly when the fact still needs saying. A toast is gone in
four seconds. Nothing else survives the scan.

WHY ONE CARD AND NOT ONE PER FEATURE. Given a corner each, two features are a
pair of competing cards and four are a notification wall on a focus-locked
bench. Sources return PendingWorkItem[] and are appended to SOURCES; the card
shows the newest and counts the rest, so the corner cost stays flat.

Three invariants, enforced where they belong rather than by a test that reads
JSX (.claude/skills/add-guard):

  - one mount — depcruise `pending-work-card-has-one-mount`. Verified it
    actually fails: a probe importing the card errored, removing it went back
    to zero.
  - org + staff scope — every source is typed PendingWorkSourceFn, so one that
    forgets staffId does not compile. The card follows the operator, so an
    org-only source would put a colleague's work in their corner.
  - a decision never gets a one-click button — PendingWorkItem is a
    discriminated union. `commit` narrows ticketNumber to string and forbids
    href; `navigate` requires href. Resolving a SHORT or a DAMAGED is a
    judgement about someone's goods, so that branch renders a link and stops.

Open receiving exceptions join as the second source, capped at 7 days.
Uncapped it is 38 rows back to mid-July, every one RETURN_NO_ORDER — an
all-time backlog that would nag forever and bury the exception raised on the
box just scanned. Within the window it is 12. Backlog belongs on a queue view
somebody triages, not on the bench.

The pure half (types + ordering) lives in pending-work-model.ts with zero
imports, because pending-work.ts reaches server-only through tenancy/db: the
client hook and the unit test cannot load it otherwise.

commits.body:
Both CI jobs died on their first step and had for several commits:

  npm error `npm ci` can only install packages when your package.json
  and package-lock.json ... are in sync.

gates) and `jsdom` in 8ba8bc90a, neither with a regenerated lock. `npm ci`

commits.subject: fix(css): resolve the legacy-colour plugin from cwd, not import.meta.url
commits.body:
The previous commit used `import.meta.url` to build an absolute path, on the
assumption it points at this file. Under Turbopack it does not: the config is

requires being run from the project root — and unlike `import.meta.url` it is
not rewritten by bundling.

`Ready in 1709ms`, `/` returns 200, no module-resolution error, and the served
stylesheet carries 185 palette vars all in hex with zero oklch. Production build
output is unaffected: 374KB main stylesheet, oklch 0, 316 rgba fallbacks intact
through minification.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: fix(css): resolve the legacy-colour plugin by absolute path for Turbopack
commits.body:
Next requires postcss plugins be named by string — it rejects a function
outright ("must be provided as a string") — and then `require()`s that string.
A RELATIVE string is resolved against whoever loads it, and Turbopack inlines
this config into `.next/dev/build/postcss.js`, so `./scripts/...` resolved
against that chunk directory and `next dev` died with:

  Cannot find module './scripts/postcss/legacy-color-fallback.cjs'

`next build --webpack` resolved the same string from the project root, which is
why four builds passed and only the dev server broke — the two bundlers do not
agree on the base, so validating with one proves nothing about the other.

Deriving the path from `import.meta.url` pins it to this file's own directory
(the project root) for every bundler and every cwd, without hardcoding anything
machine-specific: `process.cwd()` would follow wherever the command was invoked.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: fix(pwa): stop precaching build output in the committed service worker
commits.body:
public/sw.js is generated locally and committed, then shipped verbatim — PWA
compile is skipped on Vercel to avoid the webpack memory spike. Its precache
manifest named 1,409 `_next/static/chunks/<content-hash>.js` URLs, valid only
for the build that produced them. Every later deploy renames those chunks, and
workbox treats a 404 on a precached URL as a FATAL install error: the new
worker never installs, so each client stays pinned to whichever generation last
installed successfully and serves that deploy's CSS forever. That is the "old
machine still shows old classes" report — not a stale file, a worker that can
no longer install.

Fixed with two levers, because they act at different stages:
  - `exclude` filters assets harvested from the compilation. It matches the
    WEBPACK ASSET NAME (`static/chunks/x.js`) — no leading slash, no `_next`
    prefix, which is added later when the URL is built. Anchoring on
    `/_next/...` matched nothing and failed silently: two builds still emitted
    1,438 hashed entries.
  - `manifestTransforms` filters the final entries by url, catching next-pwa's
    own `additionalManifestEntries`, which bypass `exclude` entirely.

`_next/static` is content-hashed and immutable, so it is cached at RUNTIME via
a CacheFirst rule instead — same offline behaviour, no build coupling.

Measured: 1,420 precache entries / 1,409 build-hashed → 11 / 0. What remains is
stable public/ assets whose URLs survive a rebuild, so the committed worker
keeps installing across deploys.

Also moves the legacy-colour PostCSS plugin to .cjs and references it by path.
Next validates postcss config and rejects a plugin passed as a function ("must
be provided as a string"), then `require()`s the path — and an ESM default
export arrives as a namespace object postcss cannot normalize. Object form +
string path + CommonJS is the only shape that satisfies both.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: fix(css): render Tailwind v4 colours on Chrome 109 (Windows 7 floor)
commits.body:
Tailwind v4 emits its whole palette as oklch() and every /opacity utility as
color-mix(in oklab, …). Both shipped in Chrome 111; Windows 7 caps at Chrome
109, the last build Google released for it. An unparseable value invalidates
the entire declaration, so those machines lost backgrounds outright rather
than degrading — bg-blue-50 is the most-used class in this repo (406 sites),
which is why the arrival/triage surfaces render with no wash.

browserslist does NOT fix this. Measured on this tree: @tailwindcss/postcss
emits byte-identical CSS with and without targets (371,308 bytes, 532 oklch,
1,195 color-mix either way). It does not downlevel, so the rewrite has to be
ours.

This PostCSS pass runs after Tailwind and:
  - converts every oklch() literal to its exact sRGB hex (OKLCh → OKLab →
    linear sRGB), verified against known values — blue-50 lands on #eff6ff;
  - inserts a static rgba() declaration before each resolvable color-mix().
    Old engines keep the rgba and drop the line they cannot parse; modern
    engines parse both and the later color-mix wins, so they are unchanged.

Measured on src/app/globals.css: oklch 527 → 0, and 315 of 911 color-mix
declarations gain a fallback. The remainder are nested mixes or currentcolor,
which cannot be resolved at build time — those still degrade on Chrome 109,
but they are borders/rings rather than the backgrounds that prompted this.

Does not fix Safari on the 2010 iMac: Tailwind v4 emits cascade layers, which
need Safari 15.4+, and that machine caps at 13.1. It needs Chrome 116.

commits.subject: fix(receiving): procedure-gate writes are never fire-and-forget
commits.body:
Nine writes to the durable stamps the Unbox capture steps settle on
(condition_graded_at, label_printed_at, serial_absent + per-unit twins)
were spelled `void fetch(...).catch(() => {})` — the response was never
inspected. A 403, RLS rejection or dropped connection advanced the
operator step gate on a fact the database never recorded, with no toast,
no log and no console warning.

The docblocks justified this as "fire-and-forget; the server COALESCE
keeps the first write". COALESCE makes a duplicate write harmless; it
does nothing for a write that never arrived.

New waist `receiving-gate-write.ts`: apply -> persist -> inspect status
-> revert + operator reason + Retry. Batch writes attribute each failure
to its unit and revert only those, since the successes are durable.

The line-level snapshot is a required parameter with no default, per
backend-patterns.md — a defaulted snapshot is a silent opt-out at every
call site nobody visited.

Also folds in a ninth site the audit missed: UnitsExplosionDisplay
PATCHed /condition inline AND used the generic c.patch for the set path,
which never stamps condition_graded_at — so the Condition step could not
settle from that surface at all.

Guard: receiving-gate-write.guard.test.ts (14 tests) — behavioural cover
on the failure copy plus a shrink-only ratchet on the swallowed-fetch
pattern across the receiving/station trees. Verified to fail when the
pattern is reintroduced.

The per-bench ORDER counts shipped as a full-width chip row inside the KPI
band. That is the wrong home twice over: it spent a whole band of vertical
height on the densest desk in the app, and a facet that narrows ROWS belongs
beside the query that narrows them (house law 2026-08-08, enforced by
band3-find-only.guard.test.ts) — the Band-3 right zone is view toggles only.

It is deliberately NOT inside the Views menu. Views is a saved-snapshot
store (`saved_views` / useSavedViews); a facet is not a saved view. The
relationship already runs the other way and works: `packStation` is one of
To-ship's saved-view `paramKeys`, so a view REMEMBERS the bench rather than
hosting the control.

- `BenchRefineFacet` mounts in the find field's `trailingSuffix` as a

  count (empty benches included — "Station 3 · 0" is a real answer) plus

  band already reads, so it costs no extra fetch. Pre-pack lanes only.
- `togglePackStation` / `togglePackPlaced` / `clearPackPlacement` join
  `useToShipFilterActions` — the surface's ONE URL write path. That is what
  keeps `?packStation=` and `?packPlaced=` mutually exclusive; a second
  writer is exactly how those two would drift apart.
- The aggregate "At stations" KPI tile stays. It is an attention metric,
  not a facet, and it is the at-a-glance number.

commits.author: DENSENSE8
commits.subject: fix(right-rail): render a picked occupant once, not twice
commits.body:
RightRailHost derived push-vs-overlay from `frame.mode`, which lags the
occupant's push demand by one render (the demand is published in an effect,
after commit). So a push occupant like Unbox History's `detail:history`
inspector mounted in the OVERLAY branch first, then swapped to PUSH once the
frame store round-tripped — and AnimatePresence keeps the losing overlay
`motion.aside` alive through its exit. Under throttled rAF that exit never
completes, so one carton rendered TWO panels with TWO live "Delete carton"
controls.

Decide push/overlay synchronously from the occupant's own `wantsPush` intent
(the host already computes it) instead of the lagging `frame.mode`. A push
occupant now only ever mounts in the push branch — no overlay→push handoff,
no duplicate. The frame store still owns `capPx`; only the mode decision moved
local. Reordered so `wantsPush` (and its `collapsed` dependency) computes
before `isPush`; the parked-no-strip latch is preserved.

Tighten the History delete spec to assert exactly one panel (toHaveCount(1))
in place of the `.first()` workaround. Verified on the QA org (qa-desktop).
